title: The testing effect
hook: Quizzing yourself beats rereading, even though rereading feels like it works better.
peek: Students who test themselves remember far more a week later than students who reread the same material. Yet the rereaders feel more confident. Pulling a memory out, it turns out, strengthens it more than putting it in again.
lede: Most students study by rereading their notes. It feels productive: the material looks familiar and seems to be sinking in. Experiments show that trying to recall it, with a quiz, flashcards or a blank page, works much better for remembering it later. The act of retrieving a memory makes it stronger, and the effort that makes it feel harder is part of why it helps.

bullets.text: In a 2006 study, Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke had students either reread a passage several times or read it once and then try to recall it. After five minutes the rereaders did better, but a week later the recall group remembered far more.
The students who reread predicted they would remember more than the students who practised recall did. Familiarity felt like learning, so the less effective method seemed like the better one.

In a 2011 study, Karpicke and Janell Blunt compared practice recall with drawing concept maps of a science text. Recall gave better results a week later, even on questions that asked students to draw connections.
Even failing helps. Trying to answer a question before learning the answer, then seeing it, often leads to better memory than simply studying the answer, as long as the correct answer follows.
